power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Lucid dreams, sleep paralysis, and sleep-related out-of-body experiences (OBEs) are usually defined by a characteristic feature, although considerable phenomenological variability exists within each phenomenon.
We explored how different experiential features were organized across participant-level profiles within these phenomena.
Data came from an online survey completed by 389 adults who reported at least one of the three experiences.
Separate multivariate analyses were conducted within each phenomenon using multiple correspondence analysis followed by hierarchical clustering on principal components.
We examined volitional regulation, predominant affective category, and, for OBEs, embodiment-related features.
In lucid dreams and OBEs, voluntary induction, agency, and environmental control did not always occur together.
Consistent voluntary induction and consistent environmental control characterized different profiles in both phenomena.
In OBEs, predominantly positive emotions characterized profiles with different patterns of induction and agency, whereas predominantly negative emotions characterized a profile with low volition.

In sleep paralysis, predominantly negative emotions occurred across several phenomenological profiles, whereas predominantly positive emotions characterized a profile associated with vestibular-motor experiences and out-of-body feelings (OBFs).
Sleep-related OBEs also showed marked variability in bodily experience, including profiles characterized by consistent body ownership, variable embodiment, or no perceived body.
These findings provide an exploratory description of how phenomenological features are organized across participant-level profiles within lucid dreams, sleep paralysis, and OBEs.
The resulting profiles should not be considered fixed subtypes, but rather patterns to be tested in independent samples using prospective or episode-level assessments.
Lucid dreams, sleep paralysis, and sleep-related out-of-body experiences (OBEs) are usually treated as distinct phenomena, each identified by a characteristic feature.
In lucid dreaming, the dreamer becomes aware that they are dreaming while the dream continues (LaBerge et al., 1981; Voss et al., 2013).
text.formatted: In lucid dreaming, the dreamer becomes aware that they are dreaming while the dream continues <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(LaBerge et al., 1981;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Voss et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Sleep paralysis occurs at the transition between sleep and wakefulness and is characterized by a temporary inability to perform voluntary movements despite preserved awareness (Cheyne et al., 1999).
text.formatted: Sleep paralysis occurs at the transition between sleep and wakefulness and is characterized by a temporary inability to perform voluntary movements despite preserved awareness <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Cheyne et al., 1999)</ref>.

text.text: OBEs are defined by an altered self-location, in which the self is experienced outside the physical body, typically together with an extracorporeal visuospatial perspective (Blanke et al., 2004; Blanke & Arzy, 2005).
text.formatted: OBEs are defined by an altered self-location, in which the self is experienced outside the physical body, typically together with an extracorporeal visuospatial perspective <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Blanke et al., 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Blanke & Arzy, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: These defining features, however, say relatively little about the rest of the experience.

Lucid dreams vary in the degree of agency and control that accompanies lucidity (Voss et al., 2013; Stumbrys et al., 2014), sleep paralysis can include very different perceptual and emotional experiences (Cheyne et al., 1999), and OBEs show substantial variation in their circumstances of occurrence and phenomenology (Twemlow et al., 1982).
text.formatted: Lucid dreams vary in the degree of agency and control that accompanies lucidity <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Voss et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Stumbrys et al., 2014)</ref>, sleep paralysis can include very different perceptual and emotional experiences <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Cheyne et al., 1999)</ref>, and OBEs show substantial variation in their circumstances of occurrence and phenomenology <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Twemlow et al., 1982)</ref>.

text.text: The boundaries between these experiences are also not strict.
Lucid dreaming and OBEs have been found to occur in the same individuals (Blackmore, 1982).
text.formatted: Lucid dreaming and OBEs have been found to occur in the same individuals <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Blackmore, 1982)</ref>.

text.text: This is also the case for lucid dreaming and sleep paralysis, and their frequency is positively related, particularly when sleep paralysis includes vestibular-motor experiences (Denis & Poerio, 2017).
text.formatted: This is also the case for lucid dreaming and sleep paralysis, and their frequency is positively related, particularly when sleep paralysis includes vestibular-motor experiences <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Denis & Poerio, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: During sleep paralysis, participants may report floating, flying, illusory movement, or experiences of being located outside the physical body (Cheyne et al., 1999; Girard & Cheyne, 2004).
text.formatted: During sleep paralysis, participants may report floating, flying, illusory movement, or experiences of being located outside the physical body <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Cheyne et al., 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Girard & Cheyne, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: OBEs have also been reported during sleep paralysis and in relation to lucid dreaming (Campillo-Ferrer et al., 2024; Moix et al., 2025).
text.formatted: OBEs have also been reported during sleep paralysis and in relation to lucid dreaming <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Campillo-Ferrer et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Moix et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: These overlaps show that some experiential features are shared across lucid dreams, sleep paralysis, and OBEs despite the different criteria used to define each phenomenon.
In lucid dreams, awareness of dreaming and control over the dream are not equivalent.

In the Lucidity and Consciousness in Dreams scale, insight and control emerged as separate dimensions of lucid-dream experience (Voss et al., 2013), and surveys of lucid dreamers show considerable variability in active participation and the ability to influence dream events (Stumbrys et al., 2014).
text.formatted: In the Lucidity and Consciousness in Dreams scale, insight and control emerged as separate dimensions of lucid-dream experience <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Voss et al., 2013)</ref>, and surveys of lucid dreamers show considerable variability in active participation and the ability to influence dream events <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Stumbrys et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Voluntary induction, intentional action during the experience, and control over the experienced environment also refer to different aspects of volition.

OBEs may occur spontaneously or be deliberately induced (Herrero et al., 2023; Moix et al., 2025), and individuals differ in the degree of agency and control reported during the experience (Twemlow et al., 1982; Weiler et al., 2025).
text.formatted: OBEs may occur spontaneously or be deliberately induced <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Herrero et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Moix et al., 2025)</ref>, and individuals differ in the degree of agency and control reported during the experience <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Twemlow et al., 1982;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Weiler et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Initiating an episode, acting intentionally within it, and modifying the experienced environment refer to different aspects of volition, and how these aspects combine within lucid dreams and OBEs remains unclear.
Sleep paralysis provides a particularly clear example of internal phenomenological heterogeneity.

Cheyne and colleagues identified three broad groups of associated experiences: Intruder phenomena, including sensed presence and visual or auditory hallucinations; Incubus phenomena, involving bodily pressure, breathing difficulties, suffocation, or choking; and vestibular-motor phenomena, which are centered on one's own body and encompass anomalous experiences of bodily movement and out-of-body phenomenology (Cheyne et al., 1999; Cheyne & Girard, 2009).
text.formatted: Cheyne and colleagues identified three broad groups of associated experiences: Intruder phenomena, including sensed presence and visual or auditory hallucinations; Incubus phenomena, involving bodily pressure, breathing difficulties, suffocation, or choking; and vestibular-motor phenomena, which are centered on one's own body and encompass anomalous experiences of bodily movement and out-of-body phenomenology <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Cheyne et al., 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Cheyne & Girard, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Within this broader vestibular-motor domain, movement-related experiences include sensations such as floating, flying, falling, spinning, or illusory bodily movement. Cheyne and Girard (2009) further distinguished the bodily sensation of separation from, or leaving, the physical body-termed an out-of-body feeling (OBF)-from the visual experience of perceiving one's own body from an external vantage point.
text.formatted: Within this broader vestibular-motor domain, movement-related experiences include sensations such as floating, flying, falling, spinning, or illusory bodily movement. <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Cheyne and Girard (2009)</ref> further distinguished the bodily sensation of separation from, or leaving, the physical body-termed an out-of-body feeling (OBF)-from the visual experience of perceiving one's own body from an external vantage point.

text.text: These components are closely related but need not occur together, indicating that OBFs capture a specific disembodiment component of out-of-body phenomenology rather than the broader phenomenological configuration typically encompassed by an OBE.
These distinctions are also relevant to the emotional character of sleep paralysis.

Intruder and Incubus phenomena are strongly associated with fear and distress, often involving a threatening external presence or bodily threat, whereas vestibular-motor phenomena can include more positively valenced experiences (Cheyne et al., 1999; Cheyne & Girard, 2009; O'Hanlon et al., 2011; Sharpless & Kliková, 2019).

text.text: Emotional variability is also observed in lucid dreams, where affective valence is distinguishable from insight and control (Voss et al., 2013), and in OBEs, which can vary substantially in emotional tone (Herrero et al., 2023; Gallo et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Emotional variability is also observed in lucid dreams, where affective valence is distinguishable from insight and control <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Voss et al., 2013)</ref>, and in OBEs, which can vary substantially in emotional tone <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Herrero et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Gallo et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: How predominant emotional character is organized together with other phenomenological features within each of these experiences, however, remains less well understood.
Extracorporeal self-location can likewise be accompanied by different forms of bodily experience (Blanke & Arzy, 2005; Bünning & Blanke, 2005).
text.formatted: Extracorporeal self-location can likewise be accompanied by different forms of bodily experience <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Blanke & Arzy, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Bünning & Blanke, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Neurological studies of OBEs and related autoscopic phenomena have described alterations in perceived body position and movement, body completeness, and the size or shape of body parts (Blanke et al., 2004).
text.formatted: Neurological studies of OBEs and related autoscopic phenomena have described alterations in perceived body position and movement, body completeness, and the size or shape of body parts <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Blanke et al., 2004)</ref>.

text.text: Heautoscopy represents a related disturbance of bodily self-consciousness in which self-location may become ambiguous or divided between the physical body and an experienced double (Blanke & Mohr, 2005).
text.formatted: Heautoscopy represents a related disturbance of bodily self-consciousness in which self-location may become ambiguous or divided between the physical body and an experienced double <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Blanke & Mohr, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: More recent analyses further indicate that body ownership can shift dynamically during heautoscopic experiences (Szczotka & Wierzchoń, 2023).
text.formatted: More recent analyses further indicate that body ownership can shift dynamically during heautoscopic experiences <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Szczotka & Wierzchoń, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Variability also extends to the termination of OBEs: some reports describe a distinct perceived return to the physical body, whereas others end through awakening or without a consciously perceived return (Alvarado, 1997; Alvarado & Zingrone, 1998 -1999).
text.formatted: Variability also extends to the termination of OBEs: some reports describe a distinct perceived return to the physical body, whereas others end through awakening or without a consciously perceived return <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Alvarado, 1997;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Alvarado & Zingrone, 1998</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">-1999)</ref>.

text.text: Previous studies have characterized individual features of lucid dreams, sleep paralysis, and OBEs, and some have compared selected features across these phenomena (Cheyne et al., 1999; Voss et al., 2013; Denis & Poerio, 2017; Gallo et al., 2023; Weiler et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Previous studies have characterized individual features of lucid dreams, sleep paralysis, and OBEs, and some have compared selected features across these phenomena <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Cheyne et al., 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Voss et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Denis & Poerio, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Gallo et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Weiler et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Much less is known about how several features are organized together within each phenomenon.
We asked whether distinct participant-level phenomenological profiles could be identified within each of these phenomena.
Here, we examined this question using multivariate analyses conducted separately within lucid dreams, sleep paralysis, and sleep-related OBEs.
We focused on three phenomenological domains.
Volitional regulation was examined in lucid dreams and OBEs using voluntary induction, agency, and environmental control.

Predominant affective category was examined in lucid dreams and OBEs together with voluntary induction and agency, whereas in sleep paralysis it was examined together with intruder experiences, incubus experiences, vestibular-motor experiences, and OBFs.
Embodiment-related features were examined exclusively in OBEs.
Analyses were conducted separately for each phenomenon because the available variables and their theoretical relevance differed across phenomena.
Because the study was exploratory, the number of clusters was not specified in advance.
Cluster interpretation was descriptive, with the aim of identifying recurrent patterns in the reported experiences.
>Methods

text.text: This study is a secondary cross-sectional analysis of data collected as part of a broader online survey on sleep-related experiences.

Part of the sleep-paralysis and OBE data analyzed in the present study were collected as part of the same broader online survey previously reported by Herrero et al. (2023), which addressed different research questions concerning emotions, OBE induction, and sensory experiences preceding sleep paralysis and OBEs.
text.formatted: Part of the sleep-paralysis and OBE data analyzed in the present study were collected as part of the same broader online survey previously reported by <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Herrero et al. (2023)</ref>, which addressed different research questions concerning emotions, OBE induction, and sensory experiences preceding sleep paralysis and OBEs.

text.text: The multivariate analyses and phenomenological profiles reported here have not been previously published.
Spanish-speaking adults aged 18 years or older were recruited internationally through social media.
Recruitment posts were mainly directed at people with frequent dream recall or an interest in unusual sleep experiences.
The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of Alberto C. Taquini Institute for Translational Medicine Research, University of Buenos Aires.
All participants provided electronic informed consent before completing the survey.
Identifying information collected for study administration was removed before analysis, and the analytic datasets were stored and analyzed in de-identified form.
A total of 389 unique participants completed at least one of the three modules assessing lucid dreams (n = 389), sleep paralysis (n = 319), and sleep-related out-of-body experiences (OBEs; n = 216).

Because participants could complete multiple modules if they reported experiencing more than one phenomenon, these sub-samples partially overlapped (e.g., n = 187 participants completed all three modules).
Each phenomenon was analyzed separately.
The questionnaire had a modular structure, and some items were incorporated during data collection.
For each analysis, only participants with complete data for all variables included in that specific model were retained (missing responses were not imputed).

Consequently, final analytic sample sizes differed depending on the specific variables modeled: for sleep paralysis, N = 215 (affective analysis); for lucid dreams, N = 147 (volitional-regulation analysis) and N = 134 (affective analysis); and for OBEs, N = 170 (volitional-regulation analysis), N = 165 (bodily-self analysis), and N = 153 (affective analysis).
The survey was administered in Spanish.
After completing general questions, participants were presented with separate modules on lucid dreams, sleep paralysis, and sleep-related OBEs.
Each module began with a brief definition of the experience followed by a yes/no screening question.
Participants who answered affirmatively continued with the corresponding module.
Lucid dreams were described as dreams in which the person becomes aware that they are dreaming while the dream continues.
Sleep paralysis was described as an episode occurring while falling asleep or awakening in which the person feels unable to move their physical body voluntarily.
Sleep-related OBEs were described as experiences involving the sensation of being located outside the physical body and perceiving the surroundings from an external perspective.
At the end of each module, participants were invited to describe their most memorable experience of that phenomenon in their own words.
These reports were used to assess whether participants had understood the screening definition and whether the described experience was phenomenologically compatible with the corresponding category.
No participants were excluded on the basis of these descriptions.
The questionnaire items included in the present analyses were organized into three phenomenological domains: volitional regulation, predominant affective category, and embodiment-related features.
These groupings were used to structure the multivariate analyses and were not treated as psychometric scales; no composite scores were calculated.
The domains were examined only within the phenomena for which the relevant variables were available and theoretically meaningful.
Volitional regulation was analyzed in lucid dreams and sleep-related out-of-body experiences (OBEs).
Predominant affective category was analyzed in all three phenomena, together with phenomenon-specific accompanying variables.
Embodiment-related features were analyzed exclusively in OBEs.
Unless otherwise specified, questionnaire items characterized participants' experiences across the corresponding phenomenon rather than a single index episode.
Accordingly, the resulting variables are interpreted as participant-level phenomenological tendencies or experiential histories.
Their joint representation within a profile does not necessarily imply that all component features co-occurred within the same episode.
Several questionnaire items originally used more detailed categorical response scales.
Where applicable, semantically related response options were collapsed into broader analytic categories before the multivariate analyses.
These recodings were performed independently of the clustering results.
Volitional regulation was examined separately in lucid dreams and sleep-related OBEs using three categorical variables: voluntary induction, agency, and environmental control.

These variables were retained as distinct dimensions because they captured different aspects of volitional regulation: the ability to intentionally initiate an experience, the ability to act intentionally once within it, and the ability to modify the experienced environment.
Voluntary induction referred to participants' self-reported ability to intentionally induce the experience at will.

The original response options distinguished consistent successful induction, less consistent successful induction, unsuccessful induction attempts, and absence of previous induction attempts or intention to attempt induction.
For analysis, responses were grouped into three levels: consistent voluntary induction, intermittent voluntary induction, and no reported voluntary induction.

The latter category therefore did not necessarily indicate that the experience itself was spontaneous, because it also included participants who had not successfully induced the phenomenon, had never attempted to do so, or did not wish to attempt induction.
Agency was operationalized as participants' reported ability to act or move voluntarily within the experience.
Original responses distinguished consistent voluntary action, two intermediate levels reflecting variable ability to act, and complete absence of voluntary action.
The two intermediate response levels were combined for analysis, yielding three categories: consistent agency, variable agency, and absent agency.
Environmental control referred to participants' reported ability to intentionally modify aspects of the experienced surroundings, such as changing the scene or other features of the environment.
Responses were similarly represented by three analytic categories reflecting consistent, variable, or absent environmental control.
The three variables were entered jointly into the volitional-regulation analyses for lucid dreams and OBEs.
The predominant emotional character of the experience was assessed in lucid dreams, sleep-related OBEs, and sleep paralysis.
In the analytic datasets, this variable comprised three categories: predominantly positive emotions, predominantly negative emotions, and no emotions.
For lucid dreams and OBEs, predominant affective category was analyzed jointly with voluntary induction and agency.
This analysis therefore examined whether different affective profiles were embedded within different patterns of intentional induction and action during the experience.
For sleep paralysis, predominant affective category was analyzed together with four binary phenomenological-history variables: intruder, incubus, vestibular-motor, and out-of-body feelings (OBFs).
Intruder experiences referred to reports of a sensed presence, intruder, or unfamiliar agent in the immediate environment.
Incubus experiences included perceived touch or bodily pressure and sensations of breathing difficulty, suffocation, or bodily oppression.
Vestibular-motor experiences included sensations of movement, falling, flying, or floating.
OBFs referred specifically to perceived separation from, or movement outside, the physical body.
Participants could endorse more than one sleep-paralysis feature.
Each feature was coded as a separate binary variable indicating whether it had ever occurred during the participant's history of sleep paralysis.
Consequently, these variables do not establish that the endorsed features occurred simultaneously or within the same sleep-paralysis episode.
The coding of the four SP features was performed before clustering and corresponds to the phenomenological groupings used in the analytic dataset.
Embodiment-related phenomenology was examined only in sleep-related OBEs using three categorical variables: perceived embodiment, history of heautoscopic bilocation, and mode of OBE termination.

Together, these variables characterized different aspects of how participants typically experienced their bodily self across their history of OBEs rather than the structure of a single target episode.
Perceived embodiment referred to whether participants generally experienced the extracorporeal or "other" body encountered during an OBE as their own.
Responses were represented by three analytic categories: consistent body ownership, variable embodiment, and no perceived body.
Consistent body ownership indicated that an experienced body was reliably perceived as one's own.

Variable embodiment included reports in which bodily ownership or bodily presence was not consistent across experiences, as well as some atypical descriptions of embodiment such as experiencing oneself primarily as a form or point of consciousness.
The no-perceived-body category comprised responses indicating that a body was generally or consistently not experienced.
Thus, the intermediate category should not be interpreted as spatially partial ownership of specific body parts.
Heautoscopic bilocation indicated whether participants had ever experienced themselves as simultaneously located outside the physical body while also remaining in the body in bed.
This item captured the bilocation component characteristic of heautoscopy, but did not require visual perception of an autoscopic double.
Mode of OBE termination described how participants reported their OBEs typically ending.
Responses were coded as return to the physical body, awakening, or another mode of termination.

Because these variables summarized broader experiential tendencies or histories, their combination within the clustering analysis should be interpreted as a participant-level embodiment profile rather than as evidence that all three characteristics occurred together within an individual OBE.
All analyses were performed in R version 4.4.1.
Each phenomenological domain was analyzed separately within the corresponding phenomenon.
Participants with missing data in any variable included in a given analysis were excluded from that analysis.
Because some participants completed more than one experiential module, the lucid-dream, sleep-paralysis, and OBE samples partially overlapped.
No clustering analysis combined observations from different phenomena, and cluster solutions obtained for different phenomena were not compared statistically.
Multiple correspondence analysis (MCA) was performed using the MCA() function from the FactoMineR package (Lê et al., 2008).
text.formatted: Multiple correspondence analysis (MCA) was performed using the MCA() function from the FactoMineR package <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Lê et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Separate MCAs were conducted for each phenomenon and phenomenological domain.
MCA was used because all active variables were categorical.
Participants were represented according to their response profiles in a multidimensional factorial space, while response categories were positioned according to their patterns of co-occurrence.
Categories with an ordinal interpretation were treated as categorical modalities, without assuming equal distances between adjacent response levels.
For each analysis, MCA dimensions were retained until cumulative inertia reached at least 80%.
Participants' coordinates on these retained dimensions were subsequently used for clustering.
Category contributions and squared cosine values were inspected when interpreting the factorial dimensions.
Hierarchical clustering on principal components was performed on the retained MCA coordinates using the HCPC() function from the FactoMineR package.
Euclidean distances were computed across the reduced factorial space, followed by hierarchical agglomeration using Ward's minimum-variance criterion (ward.D2).
The resulting partition was subsequently consolidated via k-means clustering initialized from the hierarchical cluster centroids, as implemented in HCPC.
Cluster membership and all subsequent descriptions refer to this consolidated partition.
Candidate solutions containing between two and eight clusters were systematically evaluated.
For each solution, average silhouette width, the Calinski-Harabasz index, and the Dunn index were computed.

Because these validation metrics did not always converge on the same partition, the final number of clusters was determined by balancing the three indices against cluster sample sizes, model parsimony, and the conceptual interpretability of the response profiles.
When adjacent solutions exhibited comparable statistical support, the more parsimonious solution with fewer clusters was retained.
In the resulting hierarchical trees, fusion heights reflect the cost of aggregation under Ward's criterion-namely, the increase in within-cluster inertia (variance) upon merging.
Mergers occurring at relatively low heights denote closely aligned, highly homogeneous response profiles.

Sub-branches consolidating only at intermediate tree levels indicate clusters with broader internal variability or differentiated sub-structures, whereas major branches joining near the top of the tree demonstrate that their amalgamation would introduce substantial heterogeneity, thus justifying their separation into distinct clusters.
Clusters were characterized based on the distribution of response categories within each profile.
Category-specific v-test statistics were computed using the catdes() function in FactoMineR.
Positive v-test values indicate overrepresentation of a response category within a cluster.
Benjamini-Hochberg corrections were applied across category-level comparisons within each cluster.
Figures display only categories that were significantly overrepresented after correction (p_adj < .05).
text.formatted: Figures display only categories that were significantly overrepresented after correction (p_adj < .05).

text.text: Cluster stability was assessed using 1,000 nonparametric bootstrap resamples of the retained MCA coordinates.
For each bootstrap sample, Ward.D2 hierarchical clustering was reapplied at the selected number of clusters.

The MCA solution itself was not re-estimated within bootstrap iterations; therefore, the resulting Jaccard coefficients quantify the stability of the hierarchical clustering conditional on the factorial representation obtained from the original sample.
For descriptive interpretation, mean clusterwise Jaccard coefficients below .60 were considered indicative of weak cluster recovery (Hennig, 2007).
text.formatted: For descriptive interpretation, mean clusterwise Jaccard coefficients below .60 were considered indicative of weak cluster recovery <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Hennig, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Because bootstrap stability was evaluated for the Ward hierarchical partition, whereas cluster membership and profile descriptions were based on the final k-means-consolidated HCPC partition, agreement between the hierarchical and consolidated solutions was assessed separately.
Concordance was quantified using the adjusted Rand index (ARI), which measures agreement between two cluster partitions while correcting for agreement expected by chance.

In the figures, horizontal dendrograms illustrate the initial Ward hierarchical tree, whereas cluster membership, sample sizes, and profile descriptions correspond to the final k-means-consolidated partition.
The trees are read from right to left, progressing from individual participants or closely aligned subgroups toward broader clusters.
Merges occurring at lower linkage heights join more similar response profiles, whereas merges at higher linkage heights indicate greater dissimilarity within the hierarchical representation.

Finally, schematic illustrations were developed post hoc to visually summarize the predominant experiential features of each profile; these served strictly for presentation purposes, were not shown to participants, and were not incorporated into any statistical analysis.
Six separate clustering analyses were conducted across the three phenomena and phenomenological domains examined.
In each case, the retained hierarchical solution was consolidated through k-means, and the profiles described below correspond to the final consolidated partition.
Agreement between the initial Ward partitions and the final k-means-consolidated solutions was very high across analyses (ARI = .927-1.000), with exact agreement in four of the six solutions.

The present study explored how phenomenological features were organized across participant-level profiles within sleep-related out-of-body experiences, lucid dreams, and sleep paralysis.

Different profiles emerged within each phenomenon, showing that participants reporting the same type of experience could differ considerably in agency, control, affect, perceptual features, and bodily experience.
These profiles are descriptive and specific to the present samples.
They nevertheless provide a way of examining the internal variability of experiences that are usually identified through a single defining feature.
In lucid dreams and OBEs, voluntary induction, agency, and environmental control did not always occur together.

This is consistent with previous work on lucid dreaming showing that insight and control represent distinguishable aspects of the experience and that becoming aware of dreaming does not guarantee an equivalent capacity to influence dream events (Voss et al., 2013; Stumbrys et al., 2014).
text.formatted: This is consistent with previous work on lucid dreaming showing that insight and control represent distinguishable aspects of the experience and that becoming aware of dreaming does not guarantee an equivalent capacity to influence dream events <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Voss et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Stumbrys et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Our results add voluntary induction to this picture.
Participants who reported being able to deliberately initiate the experience were not necessarily those who reported consistent control over the environment once the episode had begun.
The same pattern was observed in OBEs, where induction and environmental control also characterized different profiles.

This is relevant because induction, agency, and control are often discussed together when describing highly volitional sleep experiences, even though they refer to different moments or aspects of the episode.
Deliberately entering an experience, acting intentionally within it, and modifying its contents therefore need not covary in a fixed manner across individuals.

The present data do not establish whether these features rely on different cognitive mechanisms, but they show that treating them as interchangeable would miss part of the phenomenological variability observed in both lucid dreams and OBEs.
Predominant emotional character also appeared in different combinations with volitional features.
In OBEs, predominantly positive emotions characterized profiles with different patterns of induction and agency.
Predominantly negative emotions characterized a profile with absent agency and no reported voluntary induction.

Previous studies have described marked variation in the emotional quality of OBEs and differences in emotional content and experiential control between OBEs and lucid dreams (Herrero et al., 2023; Gallo et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Previous studies have described marked variation in the emotional quality of OBEs and differences in emotional content and experiential control between OBEs and lucid dreams <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Herrero et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Gallo et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The present analysis adds a within-phenomenon perspective, showing that similar predominant emotional character can occur in OBEs with different patterns of induction and agency.
The affective organization of lucid dreams was less differentiated.
Predominantly positive emotions were frequent overall but did not define a particular profile, and most participants were grouped in a large variable-volition profile.
A small profile combined predominantly negative emotions with absent agency and no reported voluntary induction.
Given its small size and the more modest bootstrap recovery obtained in this analysis, this configuration should be interpreted cautiously.
Previous work has already shown that lucidity, affective valence, and dream control are not equivalent dimensions of lucid-dream experience (Voss et al., 2013; Stumbrys et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Previous work has already shown that lucidity, affective valence, and dream control are not equivalent dimensions of lucid-dream experience <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Voss et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Stumbrys et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: The present findings are compatible with that variability, although they provide limited evidence for a specific organization between predominant emotional character and volition in lucid dreams.
Sleep paralysis showed a different relationship between affect and phenomenology.

Predominantly negative emotions characterized several profiles, including profiles associated with intruder experiences and another with a broader combination of intruder, incubus, vestibular-motor experiences, and OBFs.
Predominantly positive emotions characterized a profile associated with vestibular-motor experiences and OBFs.
This organization has clear points of contact with the classic phenomenological description of sleep paralysis.

Cheyne and colleagues distinguished intruder, incubus, and vestibular-motor components, with intruder and incubus phenomena more strongly associated with fear and distress and vestibular-motor experiences encompassing phenomena such as floating, flying, illusory movement, and out-of-body experiences (Cheyne et al., 1999; Cheyne & Girard, 2009).

text.text: Subsequent studies have similarly emphasized the strong negative affect associated with sensed presence and hallucinatory experiences during sleep paralysis (O'Hanlon et al., 2011; Sharpless & Kliková, 2019).

text.text: It is noteworthy that some of these previously described associations were recovered in an exploratory multivariate analysis.
In particular, intruder experiences characterized negative profiles, whereas vestibular-motor experiences and OBFs characterized the positive profile.

At the same time, predominantly negative emotions were not restricted to a single phenomenological profile, illustrating the diversity of experiential histories that can occur under the broad label of sleep paralysis.
The sleep-paralysis variables referred to participants' broader histories of these experiences.
Features grouped within the same profile may therefore have occurred in different episodes.
The positive vestibular-motor/OBF profile cannot be taken as evidence that these experiences are accompanied by positive emotions within the same episode.
Episode-level reports would be needed to examine that association directly.
The bodily-self analysis of OBEs also showed substantial heterogeneity.
Extracorporeal self-location defines the experience, but participants differed markedly in how the bodily self was represented.
The resulting profiles included consistent body ownership, variable embodiment, and no perceived body.

Similar variability has been described in studies of OBEs and related autoscopic phenomena, in which self-location, bodily identification, perceived body position, and first-person perspective can be altered in different combinations (Blanke et al., 2004; Blanke & Arzy, 2005; Blanke & Mohr, 2005).

text.text: The present findings are consistent with this literature and suggest that extracorporeal self-location can coexist with substantially different forms of bodily experience during sleep-related OBEs.
More broadly, this variability may be informative beyond the phenomenology of OBEs themselves.

Bodily self-consciousness can be conceptualized as involving partially dissociable components, including body ownership, self-location, and first-person perspective (Blanke, 2012; Serino et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Bodily self-consciousness can be conceptualized as involving partially dissociable components, including body ownership, self-location, and first-person perspective <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Blanke, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Serino et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Dreaming provides a natural model for examining the flexibility of this configuration, as the dream self can remain embodied, assume an altered or unstable bodily form, or in some cases persist in the absence of a spatially extended body representation. Metzinger (2013), for example, draws a parallel between such "bodiless dreams" and asomatic OBEs, in which the experiencing subject is located outside the represented physical body without experiencing itself as possessing an extended bodily form.
text.formatted: Dreaming provides a natural model for examining the flexibility of this configuration, as the dream self can remain embodied, assume an altered or unstable bodily form, or in some cases persist in the absence of a spatially extended body representation. <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Metzinger (2013)</ref>, for example, draws a parallel between such "bodiless dreams" and asomatic OBEs, in which the experiencing subject is located outside the represented physical body without experiencing itself as possessing an extended bodily form.

text.text: Sleep-related OBEs may nevertheless constitute a particularly informative case within this broader range of bodily-self features.

Their defining alteration concerns self-location itself, which becomes spatially dissociated from the physical body, while the phenomenal body associated with that extracorporeal self-location may remain stable, become variable, or disappear altogether.
From this perspective, the profiles observed here may capture different ways in which body ownership and self-location can be recombined once their usual alignment is disrupted.

Rather than treating the OBE body as equivalent to the ordinary dream body, sleep-related OBEs may therefore extend the study of dream embodiment by providing a natural context in which the spatial relation between self and body is itself systematically altered.
Profiles characterized by consistent body ownership also differed according to participants' history of heautoscopic bilocation and their typical mode of OBE termination.

Two profiles shared consistent body ownership and a reported history of heautoscopic bilocation, but differed in how the experience typically ended, with one characterized by a perceived return to the physical body and the other by awakening.

Episode termination has received considerably less attention than self-location and visuospatial perspective in descriptions of OBEs, yet these findings suggest that it may contribute an additional dimension of phenomenological variability.
Heautoscopic bilocation itself requires cautious interpretation.
The item captured simultaneous self-location inside and outside the physical body, a core component of heautoscopic phenomenology, but did not require visual perception of an autoscopic double.
It therefore should not be interpreted as a measure of the full heautoscopic syndrome.

Nevertheless, the occurrence of bilocation-like experiences among individuals reporting sleep-related OBEs is theoretically relevant because heautoscopic phenomena involve disturbances in the normally unified relations among self-location, bodily identification, and perspective (Blanke & Mohr, 2005; Szczotka & Wierzchoń, 2023).
text.formatted: Nevertheless, the occurrence of bilocation-like experiences among individuals reporting sleep-related OBEs is theoretically relevant because heautoscopic phenomena involve disturbances in the normally unified relations among self-location, bodily identification, and perspective <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Blanke & Mohr, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Szczotka & Wierzchoń, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Future episode-level studies that assess these components separately could determine more precisely how bilocation, body ownership, self-location, and visual autoscopy relate to one another during sleep-related OBEs.
Taken together, the analyses show that the defining characteristic of each phenomenon leaves considerable room for phenomenological variation.

Lucid dreams differed in the way volitional features were combined, sleep paralysis included several combinations of affective and perceptual phenomena, and OBEs varied in volitional, affective, and bodily characteristics.
Similarities across analyses were also apparent, particularly in the separation between voluntary induction and environmental control in lucid dreams and OBEs.
However, the analyses were conducted independently, using partly different variables and participant subsets, and therefore do not establish a common phenomenological structure across phenomena.
Several limitations are important when interpreting these findings.
Participants were recruited through an online survey primarily directed toward individuals with frequent dream recall or an interest in unusual sleep experiences.
The samples cannot be considered representative of the general population, and the frequency of the clusters should not be interpreted as the prevalence of particular experiential profiles.
The data were retrospective and, for several variables, summarized participants' experiences across multiple episodes.
Predominant affective category likewise reflected an overall characterization rather than the emotional course of an individual event.
The questionnaire was not originally designed as a psychometric instrument for identifying latent phenomenological subtypes.

Several original response options were collapsed into broader analytic categories on semantic grounds before clustering, and the resulting solutions necessarily depend on the variables and coding decisions used.
Because some questionnaire items were introduced after data collection had begun, analysis-specific samples differed substantially in size and may not be directly comparable.
Although cluster stability was generally good and was high in several analyses, this does not establish that the same profiles will emerge in independent samples.

The lucid-dream affective analysis deserves particular caution because most participants belonged to a single profile, the remaining profiles were small, and cluster recovery was lower than in the other analyses.
Lucid dreams, sleep paralysis, and OBEs were analyzed separately, and similarities between profiles across phenomena were not tested statistically.
Direct comparisons would require common measures administered across phenomena within a design developed specifically for that purpose.
The present study provides an exploratory description of participant-level phenomenological profiles within lucid dreams, sleep paralysis, and sleep-related OBEs.
The profiles observed here capture part of the variability that exists within each experiential category and identify combinations of features that can be examined more directly in future studies.
Their reproducibility remains to be established in independent samples, ideally using prospective or episode-level assessments and common measures across phenomena.
